title: This too is for good (Taanit 21a)
hook: Nachum of Gamzu met every setback by saying this too is for good

segments.voice: Yesterday a man planted a carob tree, because his ancestors had planted for him. Your line was plant for others.

You miss the train. The coffee spills. The email you were waiting for says no. There's a split second before you react when you get to decide what this is. A disaster? An annoyance? A story you'll tell later? One sage in the Talmud filled that split second with the same three Hebrew words, every single time. Gam zu l'tovah. This too is for good. People called him Nachum Ish Gam Zu: Nachum, the this-too man.
screen: `THE TRAIN, THE COFFEE, THE NO.` → `A SPLIT SECOND TO DECIDE.` → `NACHUM, THE THIS-TOO MAN.`

segments.voice: Tractate Taanit tells it. The Jewish community wanted to send a gift to the emperor in Rome, and chose Nachum to carry it, because miracles seemed to follow him. They gave him a chest full of jewels. On the way he stopped at an inn, and in the night the innkeepers opened the chest, stole the jewels, and filled it with dirt. In the morning Nachum saw what had happened, and said: this too is for good. At the palace he opened the chest before the emperor. Dirt. The emperor was furious and ordered him killed. Then the story turns. A stranger appeared among the emperor's advisers; the Talmud says it was the prophet Elijah. Maybe, he said, this is the dirt of their ancestor Abraham, who threw dust that turned into swords. The Romans tried it against a province they had never managed to conquer, and it worked. Nachum went home honored, his chest full of treasure. One careful point. The same passage says Nachum lived with great suffering: he was blind, with no hands or feet, and his body was covered in sores. So his three words weren't a smile pasted over pain. They were a way of trusting that the story isn't finished yet. Nachum doesn't say this is good. He says this, too, is for good. The word for does a lot of work.
screen: `A CHEST OF JEWELS FOR ROME.` · `STOLEN, FILLED WITH DIRT.` · `THE DIRT BECOMES A WEAPON.` · `NOT GOOD: FOR GOOD.` · then, large: `GAM ZU L'TOVAH.`

segments.voice: Pick one small annoyance from this week, not a tragedy, just the delayed package or the canceled plan, and notice the story you told yourself about it. Then try Nachum's words: gam zu l'tovah, this too is for good. You don't have to know how; leave the ending open, and notice if anything loosens.
Nachum, called the this-too man, who met every setback with three Hebrew words: gam zu l'tovah, this too is for good, trusting the story wasn't over.
Your line: this too for the good. The ending isn't written yet. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 279 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: IT IS NOT IN HEAVEN.`

howItsDone: Gam zu l'tovah is an everyday Jewish expression, said when plans fall through; a related saying in the Talmud, attributed to Rabbi Akiva, is that everything the Merciful One does is for good.

chat.says: So Nachum thought everything bad that happens is secretly good?
options: Not quite. He said this too is for good: the story isn't finished yet.
Yes, he said bad news should be ignored, smiling until it passes.
He only said it about small things, never about real suffering.
chat.meaning: Nachum didn't say 'this is good.' He said 'this, too, is for good,' trusting the story wasn't over, even amid great suffering.

Nachum.meaning: a sage known as the this-too man

Elijah.meaning: the biblical prophet; here, a stranger among the emperor's advisers

Taanit.meaning: a Talmud tractate about fast days and prayers for rain

notes: Taanit 21a paraphrased; a parallel appears in Sanhedrin 108b–109a. Abraham's dust turning to swords is a midrashic reading of Isaiah 41:2.
Whether 'Ish Gam Zu' refers to the town of Gimzo or to his saying: the Talmud gives the saying as the reason; many scholars link it to the town. Stated in the trapdoor.
Rabbi Akiva's 'all that the Merciful One does is for good' (Berakhot 60b) is a separate saying; tradition makes Akiva Nachum's student.
The suffering detail is from Taanit 21a (the house and the bed legs in water); described briefly and without drama.
Audit (second sample): Taanit 21a says the dust was tried on a province Rome could not conquer, not 'a battle they were losing'; corrected.
